claims.claim: In UK studies, missing preferences were common; once included, the proportion preferring home was unknown.
claims.supporting_passage: Missing data were common. Across all health conditions when missing data were excluded the majority preference was for home: when missing data were included, it was not known what proportion of patients with cancer, non-cancer or multiple conditions preferred home.
claims.pico_timeframe: UK adults, 61 studies 2000-2015 / reported preference for place of death
claims.safe_wording: A review of 61 UK studies found many people's preferences were never asked or recorded. Among those recorded, most chose home, but counting the missing views, we do not know what share of people prefer home.
claims.qualifications: Must say that recorded preferences favoured home.

claims.claim: Where people were asked was related to where they said they wished to die.
claims.supporting_passage: Where patients wished to die was related to where they were asked their preference.
claims.safe_wording: Where people were asked (for example in a hospice or at home) was linked with the place they said they preferred.

claims.claim: Most people who state a preference choose home, but estimates vary widely and about 1 in 5 changed preference.
claims.supporting_passage: There was moderate evidence that most people prefer a home death-this was found in 75% of studies, 9/14 of those of high quality. Amongst the latter and excluding outliers, home preference estimates ranged 31% to 87% for patients (9 studies)... 20% of 1395 patients in 10 studies (2 of high quality) changed their preference, but statistical significance was untested.
claims.pico_timeframe: 210 studies, 33 countries / preferred place of death / change with illness progression
claims.safe_wording: A large international review found most people who state a preference choose home, but estimates in patients ranged from about 3 in 10 to nearly 9 in 10. In 10 studies, about 1 in 5 patients changed their preference as illness progressed.
claims.qualifications: Change data from few studies, mostly low quality.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Supports home as most common stated preference; post must not imply most people do not want home.

claims.claim: US survey ranked dying at home lowest of 9 attributes (Steinhauser 2000).
claims.qualifications: Not verified in this batch; old US ranking exercise.

claims.claim: Home death / preferred place achieved is a UK quality indicator.
claims.safe_wording: Do not state as fact; say 'home death is often treated as a mark of good care' as opinion only, or omit.

claims.claim: England census survey of cancer carers: over 90% gave care in last 3 months, median 69 h 30 min per week; median GBP 370 spent.
claims.supporting_passage: In all, 1504 completed surveys were returned (28.5%). Over 90% of respondents reported spending time on care-giving in the last 3 months of the decedent's life, contributing a median 69 h 30 min of care-giving each week. Those who reported details of expenditure (72.5%) spent a median £370 in the last 3 months of the decedent's life.
claims.pico_timeframe: Bereaved carers of people dying of cancer, England, deaths 1-16 May 2015 / self-reported hours and spending / last 3 months
claims.safe_wording: In a survey of 1504 family carers of people who died of cancer in England in 2015, over 9 in 10 said they gave care in the last 3 months, a median of about 69 and a half hours a week. Those who gave spending details spent a median of £370.
claims.qualifications: Say 'reported caregiving'; do not say whether hours are active care or on call (not in abstract); cancer only; 28.5% response; self-report.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Median is among respondents; possible overlap with on-call time unknown.

numbers.meaning: median spend over 3 months, among 72.5% reporting expenditure

claims.claim: Carers' contributions are often underestimated or overlooked in evaluations.
claims.supporting_passage: However, the value of care-givers' contributions is often underestimated or overlooked in evaluations.
claims.safe_wording: The authors note that carers' contributions are often overlooked in evaluations.
claims.qualifications: Authors' background statement, not a finding.

claims.claim: Most vs least deprived neighbourhoods: more likely hospital death vs home, acute hospital care in last 3 months, and not receiving specialist palliative care; gradient across quintiles.
claims.supporting_passage: Compared to people living in the least deprived neighbourhoods, people living in the most deprived neighbourhoods were more likely to die in hospital versus home (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.23-1.38, p < 0.001), to receive acute hospital-based care in the last 3 months of life (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.08-1.25, p < 0.001), and to not receive specialist palliative care (OR 1.13, 95% CI 1.07-1.19, p < 0.001). For every quintile increase in area deprivation, hospital versus home death was more likely (OR 1.07, 95% CI 1.05-1.08, p < 0.001)
claims.pico_timeframe: High-income countries, 112 observational studies / area deprivation / least deprived / place of death, acute care, specialist palliative care / last year of life
claims.safe_wording: A review of studies from high-income countries found people in the poorest neighbourhoods were more likely than those in the richest to die in hospital rather than at home, to have hospital care in their last 3 months, and less likely to get specialist palliative care. The gap grew step by step with deprivation.
claims.qualifications: Describe in words only; observational; modest effects; causes not established; mostly North American studies (53.5%).

claims.claim: Evidence that anticipatory medicines improve symptom control or prevent admissions is inadequate; professionals believe they help.
claims.supporting_passage: Healthcare professionals believe anticipatory prescribing provides reassurance, effective symptom control, and helps to prevent crisis hospital admissions. The attitudes of patients towards anticipatory prescribing remain unknown. It is a low-cost intervention, but there is inadequate evidence to draw conclusions about its impact on symptom control and comfort or crisis hospital admissions.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults at end of life in community, 34 papers
claims.safe_wording: Professionals believe 'just in case' medicines help, but research has not yet shown whether they improve comfort or prevent hospital admissions.

claims.claim: NICE NG31/QS144 recommend anticipatory prescribing; usual symptom classes covered.
claims.safe_wording: Not verified; NICE pages could not be opened.

claims.claim: On TV dramas most people given CPR survive.
claims.supporting_passage: Diem: There were 60 occurrences of CPR in the 97 television episodes... Seventy-five percent of the patients survived the immediate arrest, and 67 percent appeared to have survived to hospital discharge. Portanova: CPR was depicted 46 times in the 91 episodes, with a survival rate of 69.6%. Among those immediately surviving following CPR, the majority (71.9%) survived to hospital discharge
claims.safe_wording: In 1990s US TV dramas, about 2 in 3 people given CPR appeared to survive to leave hospital. In Grey's Anatomy and House (2010-11), about 7 in 10 survived the CPR itself.
claims.qualifications: Compare Diem's 67% (discharge) with the audit; Portanova's 69.6% is immediate survival, not discharge. Diem TV patients were mostly young with trauma.

numbers.meaning: TV patients appearing to survive to discharge, Diem 1996, n=60

claims.claim: UK in-hospital arrest survival to discharge 18.4%; 10.5% for non-shockable rhythms (72.3% of arrests).
claims.supporting_passage: Overall unadjusted survival to hospital discharge was 18.4%. The presenting rhythm was shockable (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia) in 16.9% and non-shockable (asystole or pulseless electrical activity) in 72.3%; rates of survival to hospital discharge associated with these rhythms were 49.0% and 10.5%, respectively, but varied substantially across hospitals.
claims.pico_timeframe: 22,628 adults, 144 UK hospitals / team-attended CPR / survival to discharge
claims.safe_wording: In UK hospitals, fewer than 1 in 5 adults given CPR by the hospital team survived to leave hospital. For the most common kind of arrest, about 1 in 10 did.
claims.qualifications: Unadjusted; audit data about a decade old; all ages 16+, so older frailer people likely lower (not shown here).

candidates.reason: Hoare and Gomes support the core; Steinhauser ranking and UK indicator claims not verified.
candidates.revised_angle: Where preferences are recorded, home usually comes first, but many are never asked, answers depend on where people are asked, and about 1 in 5 change their mind; so ask, record and review. Drop Steinhauser and the indicator claim.

candidates.reason: Rowland 2017 abstract supports all figures with qualifications; do not specify what hours include.
Davies 2019 supports all claims in words.
Reserve. Bowers supports evidence gap; NICE recommendation and contents not verified.
candidates.revised_angle: Present as a way to avoid delay whose benefit is not yet proven; omit NICE specifics and paramedic claims unless verified.

candidates.reason: Diem (discharge, matched outcome) vs NCAA 18.4% and 10.5%; drop frailty and rib claims.
